title: Exact planar Euclidean matching
formal: Determine, up to constant factors including logarithmic factors, the optimal deterministic worst-case running time for computing a minimum-length perfect matching of \(2n\) distinct points in \(\mathbb R^2\), for all integers \(n\geq1\), in the exact real-arithmetic model below. The output is a list of \(n\) unordered pairs of input indices, every index occurring exactly once, minimizing \(\sum_{\{i,j\}\in M}\sqrt{(x_i-x_j)^2+(y_i-y_j)^2}\) among all perfect matchings. The input consists only of the point coordinates; the complete graph is implicit.
why: Exact Euclidean matching is a basic geometric optimization primitive. Its unresolved complexity tests how far geometric structure can reduce the cost of optimization over an implicit complete graph, beyond the easier approximation guarantees.
status_note: The exact complexity gap is explicitly present in the checked April 2026 article. The bounded later-work search on 13 September 2026 found no matching resolution. The real-arithmetic model is an explicit editorial specification of the geometric task; bit complexity and approximation are separate targets.

progress.text: Varadarajan obtains an exact \(O(n^{3/2}\log^5 n)\) algorithm.
The Open Problems Project records optimal exact planar matching complexity as unresolved.
The new journal article improves deterministic approximation while continuing to identify the 1998 bound as the best exact upper bound.

importance.reason: A longstanding gap for a fundamental geometric pairing problem, connecting exact weighted matching with the algorithmic value of low-dimensional coordinates.

sentences: Given an even number of planar points, a perfect matching pairs every point with exactly one other point.
The Euclidean objective minimizes the sum of the lengths of all chosen segments.
The question is the optimal complexity of computing that minimum exactly, with bipartite matching as a related restricted variant.
Approximation algorithms can exploit geometry differently and do not by themselves settle the exact problem.
Sharper algorithms would improve a central geometric pairing primitive whose implicit complete graph contains quadratically many candidate edges.

definitions: The coordinates are arbitrary real numbers supplied in an indexed array. No general-position, bounded-spread, coordinate-precision or unique-optimum promise is made; any minimizing matching is acceptable. An algorithm is one finite deterministic program, valid for every input size, with rational program constants, no advice and no oracle. It has exact real registers and an indexed memory. A real arithmetic operation \(+,-,\times,/\) on its domain, a nonnegative square root, a comparison, a register copy, or an indexed read or write costs one step. Integer addresses and loop counters use ordinary arithmetic and comparisons on \(O(\log(n+t+2))\)-bit words after \(t\) steps, with a program-dependent constant in this word bound; there is no floor, bit extraction from reals, or operation that solves an entire optimization problem. Input access, memory operations and output are charged. Running time is the supremum of the number of steps over all valid inputs of the given size. All programs must halt and be correct on every valid input. This fixes the conventional geometric arithmetic interpretation of the source; it is not a bit-complexity question about sums of square roots. The main problem is unrestricted perfect matching: no red/blue partition is supplied.
answer_criterion: Supply a noncircular rate \(g:\mathbb N_{\geq1}\to\mathbb R_{>0}\) and a complete Lean-checked proof of matching bounds in the stated model. The upper bound must give one uniform deterministic algorithm with worst-case time at most \(C g(n)\) for all sufficiently large \(n\). The lower bound must show that every correct uniform algorithm has worst-case time at least \(c_A g(n)\) for all sufficiently large \(n\), where \(c_A>0\) and the threshold may depend on the algorithm. Constants are independent of the point configuration and \(n\). Approximate matchings, a bound only for bipartite matching, or a polynomial exponent with unresolved logarithmic factors do not meet this criterion.

context_blocks.text: The Open Problems Project asks for the optimal complexity of exact Euclidean matching in the plane and mentions the bipartite problem separately. This card retains the unrestricted objective and makes the deterministic arithmetic and worst-case conventions explicit.

A matching contains only a linear number of edges, but the coordinate input describes quadratically many possible pairs. Its objective is the sum of their Euclidean lengths; replacing lengths by squared lengths can change the minimizing matching.

Varadarajan proves an \(O(n^{3/2}\log^5 n)\) exact algorithm. The separator subroutine in the author manuscript has a deterministic implementation, so this is an upper bound for the deterministic target rather than merely an expected randomized bound.

Hougardy and Tammemaa’s April 2026 journal article still identifies Varadarajan’s bound as the fastest known exact algorithm. Their new results improve fast approximation guarantees and do not compute the exact optimum.

The same article recalls an \(\Omega(n\log n)\) lower bound for deterministic geometric approximation algorithms with approximation ratio depending only on input size. Thus the exact task has a substantial known gap even before finer logarithmic factors are considered.

The arithmetic convention matters because the objective involves square roots and comparisons between sums of lengths. Counting each such arithmetic step is different from bounding the number of bit operations needed to certify every comparison for rationally encoded points. The requested output here is an optimal pairing, not a decimal expansion of its total length.
